arXiv:1311.1748v4 [nlin.PS] 19 Feb 2014

Cross-diffusion driven instability in a predator-prey system with cross-diffusion

E.Tulumello Note: tulunora@gmail.com    M.C.Lombardo Note: mariacarmela.lombardo@math.unipa.it    M.Sammartino Note: marco.sammartino@math.unipa.it Affiliation: University of Palermo, Department of Mathematics, Affiliation: Via Archirafi 34, 90123 Palermo, Italy.
August 24, 2026
Abstract

In this work we investigate the process of pattern formation induced by nonlinear diffusion in a reaction-diffusion system with Lotka-Volterra predator-prey kinetics. We show that the cross-diffusion term is responsible of the destabilizing mechanism that leads to the emergence of spatial patterns. Near marginal stability we perform a weakly nonlinear analysis to predict the amplitude and the form of the pattern, deriving the Stuart-Landau amplitude equations. Moreover, in a large portion of the subcritical zone, numerical simulations show the emergence of oscillating patterns, which cannot be predicted by the weakly nonlinear analysis. Finally, when the pattern invades the domain as a travelling wavefront, we derive the Ginzburg-Landau amplitude equation which is able to describe the shape and the speed of the wave.


Keywords: Nonlinear diffusion, Turing instability, Amplitude equation, Quintic Stuart-Landau equation, Ginzburg-Landau equation.

1 Introduction

The aim of this paper is to investigate the process of pattern formation for the following reaction-diffusion system:

∂τU=ΓU(R−RKU−γ12V)+D1ΔU,∂τV=ΓV(−M+γ21U)+D21∇⋅(V∇U)+D2ΔV.\begin{split}\partial_{\tau}U&=\Gamma U\biggl(R-\frac{R}{K}U-\gamma_{12}V\biggl)+D_{1}\Delta U,\\ \partial_{\tau}V&=\Gamma V(-M+\gamma_{21}U)+D_{21}\nabla\cdot\left(V\nabla U\right)+D_{2}\Delta V.\end{split} (1)

Here U⁡(𝒛,τ)U(\boldsymbol{z},\tau) and V⁡(𝒛,τ)V(\boldsymbol{z},\tau), with 𝒛∈Ω⊆ℝn\boldsymbol{z}\in\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, are the population densities of preys and predators, respectively. The kinetics is of the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey type with a logistic term for the preys: RR and KK are the growth rate and carrying capacity for the prey, respectively, MM is the predator death rate, γ12\gamma_{12} and γ21\gamma_{21} are the rate of predation and the capture efficiency and Γ\Gamma gives the size of the spatial domain. The spatial motion of the two populations is described by the usual linear diffusion terms and by a nonlinear term deriving from the assumption that predators avoid zones of high prey density.

Without loss of generality, we shall consider the following dimensionless form of the system (1) for uu and vv:

∂tu=Γ​u​(r−γ​u−v)+∇2u,∂tv=Γv(−1+u)+d21∇⋅(v∇u)+d2∇2v,\begin{split}\partial_{t}u&=\Gamma u(r-\gamma u-v)+\nabla^{2}u,\\ \partial_{t}v&=\Gamma v(-1+u)+d_{21}\nabla\cdot(v\nabla u)+d_{2}\nabla^{2}v,\end{split} (2)

where

u(𝒙,t)=γ21MU,v(𝒙,t)=γ12MVwitht=Mτ,𝒙=MD1𝒛,u(\boldsymbol{x},t)=\frac{\gamma_{21}}{M}U,\quad v(\boldsymbol{x},t)=\frac{\gamma_{12}}{M}V\quad\text{with}\quad t=M\tau,\quad\boldsymbol{x}=\sqrt{\frac{M}{D_{1}}}\boldsymbol{z},\quad (3)

and

r=RM,γ=RK​γ21,d21=D21​MD1​γ21,d=D2D1.r=\frac{R}{M},\quad\gamma=\frac{R}{K\gamma_{21}},\quad d_{21}=\frac{D_{21}M}{D_{1}\gamma_{21}},\quad d=\frac{D_{2}}{D_{1}}. (4)

In what follows we shall restrict ourselves to the 1D domain Ω=[0,2​π]\Omega=[0,2\pi] on which we shall impose homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions.

System (2) belongs to a large class of models involving density depending diffusion (see e.g. [23]) or cross-diffusion to reproduce segregation effects and the creation of spatial niches [19, 26, 24]. Cross-diffusion terms should be introduced when the gradient of the density of one species induces a flux of another species. It has been shown that, for a large class of predator-prey or competitive kinetics without an autocalitic term, classical diffusion is not sufficient for pattern formation, no matter what diffusion rates are: in these cases, cross diffusion is necessary for pattern formation [15, 16, 24]. It is worth mentioning that the introduction of the cross diffusion terms, other than being simply guessed a priori, can rigorously be obtained through a self-consistent derivation anchored to the microscopic world (see [11]) or deduced from mutation and splitting of a single species (see [12, 7]). Cross-diffusion terms of the type introduced in (2) have already appeared in [8, 20, 24] (modeling prey congregation to protect from the attack of the predator), but also in other contexts like chemotaxis [19], ecology [18], social systems [10], electric circuits [5], drift-diffusion in semiconductors [6], chemical reactions [17], turbolent transport in plasmas [9], granular material [2], and cell division in tumor growth [25] and have also been extensively numerically investigated [13, 3, 14].

The plan of the paper is the following. In Section 2 we perform a linear stability analysis close to the coexistence equilibrium, showing that cross-diffusion is the necessary ingredient for pattern formation. In Section 3, through a weakly nonlinear analysis, we derive the cubic Stuart-Landau equation (in the subcritical regime, however, we have to push the analysis up to the fifth order to derive the quintic Stuart-Landau equation), which allow us to predict the shape and the amplitude of the pattern. In the subcritical region, where the linear analysis prescribes only Turing pattern with no temporal oscillations, we numerically detect the coexistence of Turing pattern with a limit cycle. These findings confirm the result that, even without interaction with either a Hopf or a wave instability, the Turing instability together with cross diffusion in a predator-prey model can give rise to spatiotemporally oscillating solutions ([21]). Oscillating Turing patterns of similar type, have been also found in [1]. Moreover, varying γ\gamma, which corresponds to moving away from the supercritical region, the oscillating pattern undergoes a series of bifurcations leading to torus, period doubling and chaos. We defer to a forthcoming paper the investigation of the transition to the chaotic dynamics of system (2), whose relevance in the modeling of natural phenomena has been pointed out by many authors [22, 4]. Finally, in Section 4 we consider the case of spatially modulated patterns, when the size of the spatial domain is large and the pattern is sequentially formed invading the whole domain as a traveling wavefront. In this case, we derive the real Ginzburg-Landau amplitude equation whose solution gives, to a good approximation, the shape and the speed of the traveling front.

2 Turing instability

In this section we shall investigate the conditions on the system (2) for the onset of Turing instability. The coexistence equilibrium for the kinetics is (u0,v0)≡(1,r−γ)(u_{0},v_{0})\equiv(1,r-\gamma) which is biologically significant if and only if r−γ>0r-\gamma>0. When it exists, the equilibrium is stable and can be an attractive node (for 0<r<γ+γ2/40<r<\gamma+\gamma^{2}/4) or an attractive spiral (for r>γ+γ2/4r>\gamma+\gamma^{2}/4). Notice that this kinetics does not exhibit any Hopf bifurcation. The linearized system in the neighborhood of (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) is:

wt=Γ​Jw+D​∇2w,w=(u−u0v−v0),\text{{w}}_{t}=\Gamma\text{J}\text{{w}}+D\nabla^{2}\text{{w}},\qquad\text{{w}}=\begin{pmatrix}u-u_{0}\\ v-v_{0}\end{pmatrix}, (5)

where

J=(−γ−1r−γ0),D=(10d21​v0d2).J=\begin{pmatrix}-\gamma&&-1\\ r-\gamma&&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad D=\begin{pmatrix}1&&0\\ d_{21}v_{0}&&d_{2}\end{pmatrix}. (6)

The dispersion relation, which gives the eigenvalue λ\lambda as a function of the wavenumber kk, reads:

λ2+(−Γ​tr​(J)+k2​tr​(D))​λ+h⁡(k2)=0,\lambda^{2}+(-\Gamma\text{tr}(J)+k^{2}\text{tr}(D))\lambda+h(k^{2})=0, (7)

where

h⁡(k2)=k4​det​(D)+k2​Γ​q+Γ2​det(J),withq=γ​d2−det(J)​d21.h(k^{2})=k^{4}\text{det}(D)+k^{2}\Gamma q+\Gamma^{2}\det(J),\qquad\textrm{with}\quad q=\gamma d_{2}-\det(J)d_{21}. (8)

For the steady state to be linearly unstable to spatial disturbances we require Re​(λ​(k))>0\text{Re}(\lambda(k))>0 for some k≠0k\neq 0. Since (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) is stable for the kinetics, one has that tr​(J)<0\text{tr}(J)<0. Moreover tr​(D)>0\text{tr}(D)>0. Therefore we are looking for those modes kk for which h⁡(k2)<0h(k^{2})<0. The only possibility for h⁡(k2)<0h(k^{2})<0 is q<0q<0, which means:

d21>γ​d2det(J).d_{21}>\frac{\gamma d_{2}}{\det(J)}. (9)

Thus, the only potential destabilizing mechanism is the presence of the cross-diffusion term, while predator linear diffusion plays a stabilizing role. The condition for the marginal stability at some k=kck=k_{c} is

min⁡(h⁡(kc2))=0\min(h(k_{c}^{2}))=0 (10)

and the minimum of hh is attained when km​i​n2=−Γq/(2det(D)).k^{2}_{min}=-\Gamma q/(2\det(D)). As shown in Figure 1, the graph of h⁡(k2)h(k^{2}) depends on d21d_{21}, which plays the role of the bifurcation parameter. Bifurcation happens at the critical value

d21c=γ​d2+2​det(J)​det(D)det(J),d_{21}^{c}=\frac{\gamma d_{2}+2\sqrt{\det(J)\det(D)}}{\det(J)}, (11)

in correspondence of the critical wavenumber

kc2=Γ​det(J)d2≠0.k_{c}^{2}=\Gamma\sqrt{\frac{\det(J)}{d_{2}}}\neq 0. (12)

For d21>d21cd_{21}>d_{21}^{c} the system admits a finite kk pattern-forming stationary instability. The unstable wavenumbers stay in between the roots of h⁡(k2)h(k^{2}), denoted by k12k_{1}^{2} and k22k_{2}^{2}, which are proportional to Γ\Gamma. Hence, to guarantee the emergence of spatial pattern, Γ\Gamma must be big enough so that at least one of the modes allowed by the boundary conditions, falls within the interval [k12,k22][k_{1}^{2},k_{2}^{2}]. Thus, the conditions under which patterns arise are:

r−γ>0,d21>d21c,r-\gamma>0,\qquad d_{21}>d_{21}^{c}, (13)

with d21cd_{21}^{c} given by (11). Since the growth rate λ\lambda crosses the zero having its imaginary part equal to zero (λ⁡(kc)=0\lambda(k_{c})=0), linear analysis predicts a stationary (Turing) bifurcation. Moreover, since I​m​(λ)≠0Im(\lambda)\neq 0 only for 0≤k<k10\leq k<k_{1}, from the results of the linear analysis we expect stationary patterns.

3 Weakly nonlinear analysis

In this Section we shall perform a weakly nonlinear analysis based on the method of multiple scales. Let ε2=(d21−d21c)/d21c\varepsilon^{2}=(d_{21}-d_{21}^{c})/d_{21}^{c} be the dimensionless distance from the threshold. For notational convenience, we shall denote with dd the bifurcation parameter d21d_{21}.

We introduce new scaled coordinates, which will be treated as distinct variables, in addition to the original ones:

T=ε2​t,X=ε​xT=\varepsilon^{2}t,\qquad X=\varepsilon x (14)

and therefore the space and time derivatives decouple as ∂t→∂t+ε2∂T\partial_{t}\to\partial_{t}+\varepsilon^{2}\partial_{T} and ∂x→∂x+ε∂X\partial_{x}\to\partial_{x}+\varepsilon\partial_{X}. At this stage we shall not consider the possibility of spatial slow modulation. This will be done in Section 4.

Separating the linear part from the nonlinear one, we can recast the system (2) for the perturbation w=(wu,wv)\text{{w}}=(\text{w}^{u},\text{w}^{v}), in the following form:

∂tw=ℒd​w+12​𝒬K​(w,w)+d​(0wv​∇2wu+∇wv⋅∇wu),\partial_{t}\text{{w}}=\mathcal{L}^{d}\text{{w}}+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{Q}_{K}(\text{{w}},\text{{w}})+d\begin{pmatrix}0\\ \text{w}^{v}\nabla^{2}\text{w}^{u}+\nabla\text{w}^{v}\cdot\nabla\text{w}^{u}\end{pmatrix}, (15)

where ℒd=Γ​J+Dd​∇2\mathcal{L}^{d}=\Gamma J+D^{d}\nabla^{2} is a linear operator depending on the bifurcation parameter dd and the bilinear operator 𝒬K\mathcal{Q}_{K}, which represents the nonlinear parts of the kinetics, is defined as:

𝒬K​(x,y)=Γ​(−2​γ​xu​yu−(xu​yv+xv​yu)xu​yv+xv​yu),\mathcal{Q}_{K}(\text{{x}},\text{{y}})=\Gamma\begin{pmatrix}-2\gamma\text{x}^{u}\text{y}^{u}-(\text{x}^{u}\text{y}^{v}+\text{x}^{v}\text{y}^{u})\\ \text{x}^{u}\text{y}^{v}+\text{x}^{v}\text{y}^{u}\end{pmatrix}, (16)

where x=(xu,xv)\text{{x}}=(\text{x}^{u},\text{x}^{v}) and y=(yu,yv)\text{{y}}=(\text{y}^{u},\text{y}^{v}). Finally, the last term in (15) is the nonlinear diffusion term.

We expand dd and w as:

d\displaystyle d =\displaystyle= dc+ε2​d(2)+O⁡(ε4),\displaystyle d^{c}+\varepsilon^{2}d^{(2)}+O(\varepsilon^{4}), (17)
w =\displaystyle= ε​w1+ε2​w2+ε3​w3+O⁡(ε4).\displaystyle\varepsilon\text{{w}}_{1}+\varepsilon^{2}\text{{w}}_{2}+\varepsilon^{3}\text{{w}}_{3}+O(\varepsilon^{4}). (18)

Accordingly, the operators ℒd\mathcal{L}^{d} and 𝒬K\mathcal{Q}_{K} can be expanded as:

ℒd\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{d} =\displaystyle= ℒdc+ε2​d(2)​(00v00)​∇2+O⁡(ε4),\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{d^{c}}+\varepsilon^{2}d^{(2)}\begin{pmatrix}0&&0\\ v_{0}&&0\end{pmatrix}\nabla^{2}+O(\varepsilon^{4}), (19)
𝒬K​(w,w)\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{K}(\text{{w}},\text{{w}}) =\displaystyle= ε2​𝒬K​(w1,w1)+2​ε3​𝒬K​(w1,w2)+O⁡(ε4),\displaystyle\varepsilon^{2}\mathcal{Q}_{K}(\text{{w}}_{1},\text{{w}}_{1})+2\varepsilon^{3}\mathcal{Q}_{K}(\text{{w}}_{1},\text{{w}}_{2})+O(\varepsilon^{4}), (20)

Substituting all the above expansions into (15) and collecting the terms at each order in ε\varepsilon, one gets a sequence of equations for the wi\text{{w}}_{i}.

At O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) we recover the linear problem ℒdc​w1=0\mathcal{L}^{d^{c}}\text{{w}}_{1}=0, whose solution satisfying the Neumann boundary conditions is:

w1=A⁡(T)​𝝆​cos⁡(kc​x),with ​ρ∈K​e​r​(Γ​J−kc2​Ddc),\text{{w}}_{1}=A(T)\boldsymbol{\rho}\cos(k_{c}x),\quad\text{with }\rho\in Ker(\Gamma J-k_{c}^{2}D^{d^{c}}), (21)

where w2​i\text{{w}}_{2i}, i=0,2i=0,2, are solutions of the following linear systems:

Γ​J​(w20)\displaystyle\Gamma J(\text{{w}}_{20}) =\displaystyle= −14​𝒬K​(𝝆,𝝆),\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4}\mathcal{Q}_{K}(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\rho}), (26)

At O⁡(ε3)O(\varepsilon^{3}) one gets:

ℒdcw3=(d​Ad​T𝝆+AG1(1)+A3G1(3))cos(kcx)+A3G3,cos(3kcx)\mathcal{L}^{d^{c}}\text{{w}}_{3}=\biggl(\frac{dA}{dT}\boldsymbol{\rho}+A\text{{G}}^{(1)}_{1}+A^{3}\text{{G}}^{(3)}_{1}\biggl)\cos(k_{c}x)+A^{3}\text{{G}}_{3},\cos(3k_{c}x) (28)

where

G1(1)\displaystyle\text{{G}}^{(1)}_{1} =d(2)​kc2​(0v0),\displaystyle=d^{(2)}k_{c}^{2}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ v_{0}\end{pmatrix},
G1(3)\displaystyle\text{{G}}^{(3)}_{1} =−𝒬K​(𝝆,w20)−12​𝒬K​(𝝆,w22)+dc​kc2​(0w20u​M+w22v−12​w22v),\displaystyle=-\mathcal{Q}_{K}(\boldsymbol{\rho},\text{{w}}_{20})-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{Q}_{K}(\boldsymbol{\rho},\text{{w}}_{22})+d^{c}k_{c}^{2}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ \text{{w}}_{20}^{u}M+\text{{w}}_{22}^{v}-\frac{1}{2}\text{{w}}_{22}^{v}\end{pmatrix},
G3\displaystyle\text{{G}}_{3} =−12​𝒬K​(𝝆,w22)+dc​kc2​(03​w22u​M+32​w22v).\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{Q}_{K}(\boldsymbol{\rho},\text{{w}}_{22})+d^{c}k_{c}^{2}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 3\text{{w}}_{22}^{u}M+\frac{3}{2}\text{{w}}_{22}^{v}\end{pmatrix}.

The solvability condition for (28) gives the Stuart-Landau equation for the amplitude A⁡(T)A(T):

d​Ad​T=σ​A−L​A3,\frac{dA}{dT}=\sigma A-LA^{3}, (29)

where the coefficients σ\sigma and LL are:

σ=−(G1(1),𝝍)(𝝆,𝝍),L=(G1(3),𝝍)(𝝆,𝝍).\sigma=-\frac{(\text{{G}}^{(1)}_{1},\boldsymbol{\psi})}{(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\psi})},\qquad L=\frac{(\text{{G}}^{(3)}_{1},\boldsymbol{\psi})}{(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\psi})}. (30)

In the region of the parameter space where the pattern can develop, provided that d>dcd>d^{c}, (see Fig. 2.a)), it is straightforward to prove that the coefficient σ\sigma is always positive. On the other hand, the Landau constant LL can be positive or negative, depending on the value of the system parameters. Thus the dynamics of the Stuart-Landau equation can be divided into two qualitatively different cases: the supercritical case, when L>0L>0, and the subcritical one, when L<0L<0. As the explicit expression of LL as a function of all the parameters is quite involved, it will not be given here; in figure 2.a) we show the numerically computed curve across which LL changes its sign.

3.1 The supercritical case

If the coefficients σ\sigma and LL in (29) are both positive, the bifurcation is supercritical. In this case the stable equilibrium of the Stuart-Landau equation is A∞=σ/LA_{\infty}=\sqrt{\sigma/L} and the asymptotic in time behavior of the solution is given by:

w=ε​𝝆​σL​cos⁡(kc​x)+ε2​σL​(w20+w22​cos⁡(2​kc​x))+O⁡(ε3),\text{{w}}=\varepsilon\boldsymbol{\rho}\sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{L}}\cos(k_{c}x)+\varepsilon^{2}\frac{\sigma}{L}(\text{{w}}_{20}+\text{{w}}_{22}\cos(2k_{c}x))+O(\varepsilon^{3}), (31)

where 𝝆\boldsymbol{\rho} is defined by (22) and w2​i\text{{w}}_{2i}, i=0,2i=0,2, are the solutions of the systems (26)-(27). For the above solution to satisfy the Neumann boundary conditions, kck_{c} should be an integer or semi-integer. We therefore define k¯c\bar{k}_{c} as the first integer or semi-integer to become unstable as dd crosses its critical value dcd_{c}, and take as the weakly nonlinear approssimation equation (31) in which kck_{c} is replaced by k¯c\bar{k}_{c}.

In figure 2.b) we show the comparison, for two different values of ε\varepsilon, between the stationary state predicted by the weakly nonlinear analysis (dotted line) and the stationary state reached from a random perturbation of the homogeneous equilibrium (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}), computed by solving numerically the system (2) (solid line). Notice that in the weakly nonlinear solution, we have choosen d(2)=dcd^{(2)}=d^{c}, so that we measure the deviation from the critical value in relation to dcd^{c}. Numerical results are in perfect agreement with what the weakly nonlinear analysis predicts. Infact, as the error is O⁡(ε3)O(\varepsilon^{3}), the distance evaluated in L2L^{2} norm between the weakly nonlinear approssimation and the numerical solution, becomes an eighth as ε\varepsilon is halved. On the left, in which we have choosen ε=0.15\varepsilon=0.15, the distance is about 3.78×10−33.78\times 10^{-3}, on the rigth, for a larger deviation from the bifurcation value, the distance is about 2.06×10−22.06\times 10^{-2} and ε=0.3\varepsilon=0.3.

Thus in this case (σ,L>0\sigma,L>0) weakly nonlinear analysis is able to predict the stationary nature of the instability which leads to pattern and the form and the amplitude of the pattern: we obtain stationary patterns both in spiral and node case.

3.2 The subcritical case

When LL is negative, the bifurcation is subcritical: in this case the weakly nonlinear expansion has to be pushed up to the fifth order. We therefore introduce the multiple time scales TT and T1T_{1} as follows:

t=Tε2+T1ε4+…,t=\frac{T}{\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{T_{1}}{\varepsilon^{4}}+\dots, (32)

from which the time derivative decouples as ∂t→∂t+ε2∂T+ε4∂T1\partial_{t}\to\partial_{t}+\varepsilon^{2}\partial_{T}+\varepsilon^{4}\partial_{T_{1}}, and expand dd and w up to the fifth order in ε\varepsilon.

Substituting these expansions into (15), up to O⁡(ε3)O(\varepsilon^{3}) we obtain the same equations presented in Section 3. At O⁡(ε3)O(\varepsilon^{3}), solvability condition ⟨G,𝝍~⟩=0\Braket{\text{{G}},\boldsymbol{\tilde{\psi}}}=0 for (28) leads again to (29) for the amplitude, although now the derivative with respect to TT is a partial derivative, being A=A⁡(T,T1)A=A(T,T_{1}). w3=(A​w31+A3​w32)​cos⁡(kc​x)+A3​w33​cos⁡(3​kc​x),\text{{w}}_{3}=(A\text{{w}}_{31}+A^{3}\text{{w}}_{32})\cos(k_{c}x)+A^{3}\text{{w}}_{33}\cos(3k_{c}x), (33)

where w3​i\text{{w}}_{3i}, i=1,2,3i=1,2,3, are solutions of the following linear systems:

(Γ​J−9​kc2​Ddc)​(w33)\displaystyle(\Gamma J-9k_{c}^{2}D^{d^{c}})(\text{{w}}_{33}) =\displaystyle= G3.\displaystyle\text{{G}}_{3}.

At O⁡(ε4)O(\varepsilon^{4}) the resulting equation is:

ℒdc​w3=2​A​∂A∂T​w20+A2​H0(2)+A4​H0(4)++(2A∂A∂Tw22+A2H2(2)+A4H2(2))cos(2kcx)+A4H4cos(4kcx),\mathcal{L}^{d^{c}}\text{{w}}_{3}=2A\frac{\partial A}{\partial T}\text{{w}}_{20}+A^{2}\text{{H}}_{0}^{(2)}+A^{4}\text{{H}}_{0}^{(4)}+\\ +\biggl(2A\frac{\partial A}{\partial T}\text{{w}}_{22}+A^{2}\text{{H}}_{2}^{(2)}+A^{4}\text{{H}}_{2}^{(2)}\biggl)\cos(2k_{c}x)+A^{4}\text{{H}}_{4}\cos(4k_{c}x), (34)

where H0(2)\text{{H}}_{0}^{(2)}, H0(4)\text{{H}}_{0}^{(4)}, H2(2)\text{{H}}_{2}^{(2)}, H2(4)\text{{H}}_{2}^{(4)}, H4\text{{H}}_{4} are explicitly computed in terms of the system parameters. As the expressions are quite involved, for conciseness we shall not give them here. The solvability condition for (34) is automatically satisfied and the solution is:

w4=A2​w40+A4​w41+(A2​w42+A4​w43)​cos⁡(2​kc​x)+A4​w44​cos⁡(4​kc​x),\text{{w}}_{4}=A^{2}\text{{w}}_{40}+A^{4}\text{{w}}_{41}+(A^{2}\text{{w}}_{42}+A^{4}\text{{w}}_{43})\cos(2k_{c}x)+A^{4}\text{{w}}_{44}\cos(4k_{c}x), (35)

where the w4​i\text{{w}}_{4i}, i=0,…,4i=0,\dots,4, are obtained by solving the following linear systems:

(Γ​J)​(w40)\displaystyle(\Gamma J)(\text{{w}}_{40}) =\displaystyle= 2​σ​w20+H0(2),\displaystyle 2\sigma\text{{w}}_{20}+\text{{H}}_{0}^{(2)},
(Γ​J)​(w41)\displaystyle(\Gamma J)(\text{{w}}_{41}) =\displaystyle= −2​L​w20+H0(4),\displaystyle-2L\text{{w}}_{20}+\text{{H}}_{0}^{(4)},
(Γ​J−4​kc2​Ddc)​(w42)\displaystyle(\Gamma J-4k_{c}^{2}D^{d^{c}})(\text{{w}}_{42}) =\displaystyle= 2​σ​w22+H2(2),\displaystyle 2\sigma\text{{w}}_{22}+\text{{H}}_{2}^{(2)},
(Γ​J−4​kc2​Ddc)​(w43)\displaystyle(\Gamma J-4k_{c}^{2}D^{d^{c}})(\text{{w}}_{43}) =\displaystyle= −2​L​w22+H2(4),\displaystyle-2L\text{{w}}_{22}+\text{{H}}_{2}^{(4)},
(Γ​J−16​kc2​Ddc)​(w44)\displaystyle(\Gamma J-16k_{c}^{2}D^{d^{c}})(\text{{w}}_{44}) =\displaystyle= H4.\displaystyle\text{{H}}_{4}.

At O⁡(ε5)O(\varepsilon^{5}) we finally obtain:

ℒdcw3=(∂A∂T1𝝆+∂A∂Tw31+3A2∂A∂Tw32+AI1+A3I1(3)+A5I1(5))cos(kcx)++(3A2∂A∂Tw33+A3I3(3)+A5I3(5))cos(3kcx)+A5I5(5)cos(5kcx),\mathcal{L}^{d^{c}}\text{{w}}_{3}=\biggl(\frac{\partial A}{\partial T_{1}}\boldsymbol{\rho}+\frac{\partial A}{\partial T}\text{{w}}_{31}+3A^{2}\frac{\partial A}{\partial T}\text{{w}}_{32}+A\text{{I}}_{1}+A^{3}\text{{I}}_{1}^{(3)}+A^{5}\text{{I}}_{1}^{(5)}\biggl)\cos(k_{c}x)+\\ +\biggl(3A^{2}\frac{\partial A}{\partial T}\text{{w}}_{33}+A^{3}\text{{I}}_{3}^{(3)}+A^{5}\text{{I}}_{3}^{(5)}\biggl)\cos(3k_{c}x)+A^{5}\text{{I}}_{5}^{(5)}\cos(5k_{c}x), (36)

where I1\text{{I}}_{1}, I1(3)\text{{I}}_{1}^{(3)}, I1(5)\text{{I}}_{1}^{(5)} I3(3)\text{{I}}_{3}^{(3)}, I3(5)\text{{I}}_{3}^{(5)}, I5(5)\text{{I}}_{5}^{(5)} are explicitly computed in terms of the system parameters. The solvability condition for (36) is

∂A∂T1=A​σ~−A3​L~+A5​Q~,\frac{\partial A}{\partial T_{1}}=A\tilde{\sigma}-A^{3}\tilde{L}+A^{5}\tilde{Q}, (37)

where the coefficients are

σ~=−(σ​w31+I1,𝝍)(𝝆,𝝍),L~=(−L​w31+3​σ​w32+I1(3),𝝍)(𝝆,𝝍),Q~=(3​L​w32−I1(5),𝝍)(𝝆,𝝍).\begin{split}\tilde{\sigma}&=-\frac{(\sigma\text{{w}}_{31}+\text{{I}}_{1},\boldsymbol{\psi})}{(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\psi})},\\ \tilde{L}&=\frac{(-L\text{{w}}_{31}+3\sigma\text{{w}}_{32}+\text{{I}}_{1}^{(3)},\boldsymbol{\psi})}{(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\psi})},\\ \tilde{Q}&=\frac{(3L\text{{w}}_{32}-\text{{I}}_{1}^{(5)},\boldsymbol{\psi})}{(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\psi})}.\end{split} (38)

Adding up (29) to (37), one gets the quintic Stuart-Landau equation

∂A∂T=σ¯​A−L¯​A3+Q¯​L5\frac{\partial A}{\partial T}=\bar{\sigma}A-\bar{L}A^{3}+\bar{Q}L^{5} (39)

where:

σ¯=σ+ε2​σ~,L¯=L+ε2​L~,Q¯=ε2​Q~.\bar{\sigma}=\sigma+\varepsilon^{2}\tilde{\sigma},\qquad\bar{L}=L+\varepsilon^{2}\tilde{L},\qquad\bar{Q}=\varepsilon^{2}\tilde{Q}. (40)

In the subcritical case, namely when σ¯>0\bar{\sigma}>0 and L¯<0\bar{L}<0, and when Q¯<0\bar{Q}<0, the study of the equilibria of (39) shows that there are two real stable equilibria, A∞,±=±L¯−L¯2−4​σ¯​Q¯2​Q¯A_{\infty,\pm}=\pm\sqrt{\frac{\bar{L}-\sqrt{\bar{L}^{2}-4\bar{\sigma}\bar{Q}}}{2\bar{Q}}}, which represent the asymptotic values of the amplitude. We can distinguish three zones: for d>dcd>d^{c} the only stable equilibria are A∞,±A_{\infty,\pm} and the origin is unstable. For ds<d<dcd^{s}<d<d^{c} three different stable equilibra coexist: A∞,±A_{\infty,\pm} and the origin. Moreover there are two other equilibria which are unstable. Finally for d<dsd<d^{s} the only stable equilibrium is the origin. The existence of different stable states, in corrispondence of a single value of dd, allows for the possibility of hysteresis when varying dd, as the numerical simulations confirm. In Figure 3 we show a comparison between the weakly nonlinear approximation and the numerical solution of the sistem (2). On the rigth we show the bifurcation diagram as a function of dd.

However, while in the subcritical region which is close to the supercritical one the weakly nonlinear analysis is able to predict the form of the patterns which are still stationary, as γ\gamma becomes smaller, going deeper into the subcritical region, numerical simulations show the emergence of non-stationary oscillating pattern, whose basic form is still predicted by the weakly nonlinear analysis. As the parameter γ\gamma is further decreased, the emergence of spatiotemporal chaos is recorded. To provide further insights into how the pattern changes as the parameter γ\gamma is varied, we have used the XPPAUT software package, solving the system (2) with a finite-difference scheme, and calculating the corresponding bifurcation diagram with the included sofware AUTO. Using a mesh of 5050 nodes, we get a set of 100100 ODEs solved through the stiff integrator CVODE. In Fig.4.a) the numerically calculated bifurcation diagram of the central point of the species uu, u⁡(25)u(25), is shown for the following values of the parameters: r=0.85r=0.85, Γ=10\Gamma=10, d2=1d_{2}=1, d21=2.269d_{21}=2.269. The spatially uniform steady state loses its stability at γ=0.03217\gamma=0.03217 through a subcritical pitchfork bifurcation. The bifurcating branch becomes stable at γ=0.06343\gamma=0.06343 (Turing pattern) and undergoes a secondary Hopf bifurcation at γ=0.06153\gamma=0.06153 (oscillatory Turing pattern). We remark the fact that, in this subset of the Turing space, no Hopf bifurcation is expected on the basis of the linear stability analysis. At smaller values of γ\gamma, the limit cycle loses stability and a torus bifurcation occurs at γ=0.05273\gamma=0.05273. For smaller values of γ\gamma, chaotic oscillations are finally observed (see Fig(4).b) on the right). We believe that this bifurcation diagram is consistent with well-known scenarios of routes to chaos, whose details are the subject of current investigation and will be discussed in a forthcoming paper.

4 Traveling fronts

When the size of the physical domain is large the pattern is formed sequentially and invades the entire domain as a travelling wavefront. To describe this phenomena one has to take into account the fast and the slow spatial dependence of the modulation, introducing in the weakly nonlinear analysis the slow spatial scale XX defined in (14). Consequently one determines the expressions for the operators that appear in (15). At O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) we recover the linear problem Ldc​w1=0L^{d^{c}}\text{{w}}_{1}=0 where Ldc=ΓJ+Dd∂x​xL^{d^{c}}=\Gamma J+D^{d}\partial_{xx} is the fast part of the linear operator ℒd\mathcal{L}^{d}. The solution is:

w1=A⁡(X,T)​𝝆​cos⁡(kc​x),\text{{w}}_{1}=A(X,T)\boldsymbol{\rho}\cos(k_{c}x), (41)

when 𝝆\boldsymbol{\rho} is given in (22) and AA is still arbitrary, as before.

At O⁡(ε2)O(\varepsilon^{2}) the resulting equation is

and the solvability condition is automatically satisfied. The solution is:

where w2​i\text{{w}}_{2i}, i=0,2i=0,2, and wX​1\text{{w}}_{X1} are solutions of the following linear systems:

Γ​J​(w20)\displaystyle\Gamma J(\text{{w}}_{20}) =\displaystyle= −14​𝒬K​(𝝆,𝝆),\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4}\mathcal{Q}_{K}(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\rho}),
(Γ​J−4​kc2​Ddc)​(w22)\displaystyle(\Gamma J-4k_{c}^{2}D^{d^{c}})(\text{{w}}_{22}) =\displaystyle= −14​𝒬K​(𝝆,𝝆)+dc​kc2​(0M),\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4}\mathcal{Q}_{K}(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\rho})+d^{c}k_{c}^{2}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ M\end{pmatrix},
(Γ​J−kc2​Ddc)​(wX​1)\displaystyle(\Gamma J-k_{c}^{2}D^{d^{c}})(\text{{w}}_{X1}) =\displaystyle= 2​kc​Ddc​𝝆.\displaystyle 2k_{c}D^{d^{c}}\boldsymbol{\rho}.

At O⁡(ε3)O(\varepsilon^{3}) we find:

Ldcw3=(∂A∂T𝝆+∂2A∂X2𝓖(X​X)1+A𝓖(1)1+A3𝓖(3)1)cos(kcx)++A3𝓖3cos(3kcx)+(A∂A∂X𝓖(1​X)2)sen(2kcx)L^{d^{c}}\text{{w}}_{3}=\biggl(\frac{\partial A}{\partial T}\boldsymbol{\rho}+\frac{\partial^{2}A}{\partial X^{2}}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{(XX)}_{1}+A\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{(1)}_{1}+A^{3}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{(3)}_{1}\biggl)\cos(k_{c}x)+\\ +A^{3}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}_{3}\cos(3k_{c}x)+\biggl(A\frac{\partial A}{\partial X}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{(1X)}_{2}\biggl)sen(2k_{c}x) (44)

and

∂A∂T=ν​∂2A∂X2+σ​A−L​A3,\frac{\partial A}{\partial T}=\nu\frac{\partial^{2}A}{\partial X^{2}}+\sigma A-LA^{3}, (45)

where σ\sigma and LL are given by (30). The diffusion coefficient ν\nu is given by:

ν=(2​kc​Ddc​wX​1+Ddc​𝝆,𝝍)(𝝆,𝝍),\nu=\frac{(2k_{c}D^{d^{c}}\text{{w}}_{X1}+D^{d^{c}}\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\psi})}{(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\psi})}, (46)

where ψ\psi is given by (24) and (⋅,⋅)(\cdot,\cdot) is the standard scalar product.

The Real Ginzburg-Landau equation is able to describe the invasion of the pattern of the entire domain, as its solution is the evelope of the pattern.

In figure 5 we show, at different times, the pattern that forms from a localized perturbation of the equilibrium.
